title: Prove the write is actually happening before blaming the app
explanation: `paymentd-log hello` followed by `cat /var/log/paymentd/paymentd.log` still shows nothing. That round-trip matters: it confirms the logger runs without error and the file path resolves, so the failure isn't a crashing app or a missing path — writes are succeeding somewhere, they just aren't landing where you'd expect to read them back.

title: A file that swallows every write without complaint is a strong signal, not a mystery
explanation: `ls -l /var/log/paymentd/paymentd.log` shows it isn't a regular file at all — it's a symlink to `/dev/null`. Anything appended to `/dev/null` is accepted and immediately discarded by the kernel; there's no error to see because, from the writer's perspective, the write genuinely succeeded.

title: Recognize the pattern, not just the symptom
explanation: Pointing a noisy log at `/dev/null` is a real, if crude, way people make a disk-space alert stop firing — it trades away the ability to debug anything for a quiet dashboard. Once you see the symlink target, the history of the box ("someone fixed a disk-space alert") stops being a red herring and becomes the explanation.

title: Replace the symlink with a real file, not just a differently-named one
explanation: `sudo rm /var/log/paymentd/paymentd.log && sudo touch /var/log/paymentd/paymentd.log` removes the dead symlink and creates an ordinary file in its place, so subsequent appends actually persist bytes to disk instead of being routed to the null device.

title: Verify with the same command that first proved the bug
explanation: `paymentd-log test && cat /var/log/paymentd/paymentd.log` now shows the line, confirming writes are landing in a real file — the same check from step 1, now passing.

title: The durable answer to log growth is rotation, not a black hole
explanation: The underlying problem that led to this hack — a log growing until disk fills up — still needs a real fix. `logrotate` bounds a log's size and age without destroying the ability to read it; redirecting to `/dev/null` should never be the tool for that job.
